fetched_contents.text: Modelling drug-induced cellular perturbation responses with a biologically informed dual-branch transformer Main Drug discovery is shifting from the traditional ‘one-drug–one-target’ paradigm to a more complex ‘one-drug–multiple-targets’ framework1, which stems from the realization that drugs often interact with multiple molecular targets and pathways, triggering complex signalling cascades that result in diverse phenotypic outcomes. This shift necessitates understanding genome-wide perturbation effects to elucidate mechanisms of action (MoA) and optimize therapy. To this end, researchers have increasingly turned to large-scale perturbational profiles across compounds, which facilitate the identification of high-affinity targets and context-specific effectors2,3. However, progress remains limited by the scarcity of high-quality perturbation data—particularly in clinical settings—and by confounding factors within perturbation profiles that obscure mechanistic insights. Deep learning approaches have emerged as powerful tools in this domain, enabling the mapping of broader perturbation spaces from limited observations. To achieve this, a primary challenge lies in effectively representing context-specific pre- and post-perturbation states from noisy high-throughput sequencing data. Early efforts primarily focused on autoencoder-based methods. Pioneering works, such as CPA4 and chemCPA5, leveraged the autoencoder’s denoising capabilities with an adversarial network to decouple and reconstruct the perturbation profiles. Building on this, TranSiGen6 and PRnet7 introduced variational autoencoders (VAEs)8, showing improved generalization across cellular contexts. Although effective at eliminating confounders, these methods risk over-denoising, which can obscure critical biological information. Another line of research, including DeepCE9 and CIGER10, explored attention-based architectures to model gene–drug interactions but overlooked the cellular context, yielding suboptimal results. Although the advent of single-cell large models has advanced the characterization of cellular context11,12,13, they struggle with zero-shot adaptation of the post-treatment space14,15. This motivates our approach, which separately addresses pre- and post-perturbation states. Another fundamental challenge is how to translate chemical perturbations into biological perturbation signals. State-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches typically concatenate chemical and cellular features, capturing global-cell-state alterations but failing to resolve gene-specific responses. This limitation necessitates advanced fusion strategies that integrate prior knowledge (for example, drug–target interactions (DTIs)) to bridge chemical and biological spaces. A further gap is the inadequate modelling of the well-established dose- and time-dependent nature of drug effects16,17. Previous attempts have relied on simplistic encodings (for example, one-hot encoding), which is insufficient for modelling nonlinear dose–response relationships (for example, inverted U-shaped curves)18, restricting a full understanding of transcriptional pharmacodynamics. To address these challenges, we introduce XPert, a transformer-based19 solution that predicts drug-induced transcriptional perturbations by jointly modelling cellular contexts, multiscale drug properties and dose–time dynamics. XPert features a dual-branch architecture that concurrently captures intrinsic gene–gene interactions and extrinsic chemical perturbation effects. This architecture is further augmented by a knowledge-informed heterogeneous graph (HG)20 to bridge chemical–biological spaces and by condition tokens that encode nonlinear dose–time responses. XPert excels in diverse scenarios, including generalization to unseen drugs and cells and multi-dose–multi-time (mdmt) predictions. It also supports a pretrain–fine-tune framework that extends large-scale preclinical data for clinical predictions. By enabling precise in silico modelling of perturbation dynamics across different scales, XPert establishes a transformative tool for preclinical drug discovery and personalized therapeutic development. Results Overview of XPert XPert is a transformer-based model designed to predict drug-induced transcriptional perturbation effects. Given the unperturbed cell gene expression and perturbation attributes, it simultaneously outputs the post-perturbation cell expression (xpert) and the difference between post- and pre-perturbation gene expression (xdeg = xpert – xbase). XPert leverages a dual-branch architecture to encode both pre- and post-perturbation cell states (Fig. 1). The base encoder, built with stacked self-attention layers, models complex gene–gene interactions under diverse cellular contexts, whereas the perturb encoder branch uses cross-attention to capture cell–drug interactions and condition-dependent perturbation effects. Each cell is represented as a ‘sentence’ of gene tokens, along with a \(< \mathrm{cls} >\) token representing the global cell state. Each gene token is initialized with its functional representation and binned expression value, and is then dynamically refined based on regulatory interactions with other genes and the constraints of the perturbation (Methods). XPert also models four key perturbation attributes: drug’s chemical properties, biological properties, perturbation time and dosage. All features are tokenized and fed into the model. Chemical features are extracted using UniMol21, a powerful three-dimensional (3D) molecular model. fetched_contents.text: Multi-Omics Alleviates the Limitations of Panel Sequencing for Cancer Drug Response Prediction Abstract Simple Summary Cancer is a complex, heterogeneous collection of diseases with hundred of different subtypes. Genomic aberrations that are primarily thought to be the root causes of different cancers have been clinically used as evidence for both the diagnosis and also matching individual patients to proper treatment options. However, the complexity of cancer manifests itself differently in each patient when inspected at the molecular level. Even patients with the same cancer type rarely have identical root causes for the same disease. Without an extensive molecular profile of a patient, it has been challenging to match the patients to the best treatment options. To remedy this, comprehensive genomic profiling panels have been developed to monitor hundreds of genes for a given patient, which has helped broaden the treatment options for patients. However, genomic aberrations detected in such panels still do not reflect the full complexity of how a tumour responds to cancer drugs. In this study, we demonstrate that using an additional layer of molecular information (called the transcriptome) on top of genomic aberrations that can be detected with cancer gene panels can provide significant improvements in predicting the cancer drug response in pre-clinical cancer models. Thus, this study serves as a push towards incorporating the transcriptome measurements more routinely in (pre-)clinical practice. Abstract Comprehensive genomic profiling using cancer gene panels has been shown to improve treatment options for a variety of cancer types. However, genomic aberrations detected via such gene panels do not necessarily serve as strong predictors of drug sensitivity. In this study, using pharmacogenomics datasets of cell lines, patient-derived xenografts, and ex vivo treated fresh tumor specimens, we demonstrate that utilizing the transcriptome on top of gene panel features substantially improves drug response prediction performance in cancer. Keywords: multi-omics, cancer, drug response prediction, pharmacogenomics, panel sequencing 1. Introduction Cancer is a collection of diseases characterized by abnormal cellular growth and the invasion of other body parts. It affected 19 million people in 2020 and was the cause of 9.5 million deaths that year alone [1]. Cancer has been primarily considered to be a disease of the genome, where the accumulation of alterations is the underlying cause of the transformation of normal cells into malignant cancerous cells with survival and proliferation advantages [2]. Genetic alterations of this kind have been studied to understand the mechanisms of cancer and to develop targeted therapies. The latter and companion diagnostic tools have transformed oncology [3], promising more precise treatments tailored to tumors’ genetic profiles. Various targeted therapies have been successfully developed to counteract the defects in the molecular machinery borne out of such oncogenic mutations [4,5,6]. To this date, most of the markers approved for targeted therapy decisions are single-gene markers [7]. It has thus become crucial to develop accurate, sensitive, and high-throughput genomic assays to accommodate the increasingly genotype-based therapeutic approaches. Commercial companies, such as Foundation Medicine, as well as large cancer research centers, such as Memorial Sloan Kettering and Dana Farber, have produced their panel sequencing assays to guide therapy for cancer patients [8]. These techniques examine genes that are frequently mutated in cancer to assess mutations and copy number variations. Especially for diagnostics, the approved methods for targeted drugs are usually the presence or absence of the mutations. Therefore, the assay developers focus primarily on mutation calling accuracy as a metric of the usefulness and accuracy of the assay [8]. Although comprehensive genomic profiling using cancer gene panels has demonstrated value in broadening the treatment options for patients based on matching a patient’s genomic lesions to cancer driver gene aberrations associated with FDA-approved treatment indications [8,9], the presence/absence of mutations in such genes does not necessarily translate into improved predictive power for estimating the patient’s response to the potential treatments. While for some drugs the variation in drug response can be explained by a very specific mutation (for instance, BRAF V600E mutation is a strong predictor for response to Vemurafenib in metastatic melanoma [4]), for many drugs the knowledge of the mechanism of action is missing. This is because many drugs are discovered via phenotypic screening of model systems rather than target-based approaches [10]. Of note, such single mutation markers for a given cancer type are not necessarily good markers for other cancer types. For instance, BRAF V600E, while a good predictor for metastatic melanoma, is a poor predictor of response in metastatic colorectal cancer [11]. More importantly, the latest compilation of the hallmarks of cancer recognized in the field includes factors such as the non-mutational epigenetic aberrations, the involvement of the immune system in the tumor microenvironment, and the composition of the microbiome along with genomic defects [12]. These layers of information cannot be sufficiently captured by focusing on the restricted set of genomic alterations and necessitate other data modalities. Among those, transcriptome profiling—besides being a cheap and accessible option in terms of logistics—has been shown to yield strong predictors of drug response [13,14,15]. The importance of drug toxicity assessment lies in ensuring the safety and efficacy of the pharmaceutical compounds. Predicting toxicity is crucial in drug development and risk assessment. This study compares the performance of GPT-4 and GPT-4o with traditional deep-learning and machine-learning models, WeaveGNN, MorganFP-MLP, SVC, and KNN, in predicting molecular toxicity, focusing on bone, neuro, and reproductive toxicity. The results indicate that GPT-4 is comparable to deep-learning and machine-learning models in certain areas. We utilized GPT-4 combined with molecular docking techniques to study the cardiotoxicity of three specific targets, examining traditional Chinese medicinal materials listed as both food and medicine. This approach aimed to explore the potential cardiotoxicity and mechanisms of action. The study found that components in Black Sesame, Ginger, Perilla, Sichuan Pagoda Tree Fruit, Galangal, Turmeric, Licorice, Chinese Yam, Amla, and Nutmeg exhibit toxic effects on cardiac target Cav1.2. The docking results indicated significant binding affinities, supporting the hypothesis of potential cardiotoxic effects.This research highlights the potential of ChatGPT in predicting molecular properties and its significance in medicinal chemistry, demonstrating its facilitation of a new research paradigm: with a data set, high-accuracy learning models can be generated without requiring computational knowledge or coding skills, making it accessible and easy to use. Large models are currently being used to represent individual differences in computational drug-effect studies, but they do so in ways that still reflect important tradeoffs between population-level generalization and personalized prediction.

The evidence shows that population pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PKPD) analysis is explicitly designed to individualize drug choice and dosing regimen, and that population PK studies are used to identify differences in drug safety and support dose selection, efficacy, and safety assessments across individuals [N3-R1][N3-R5]. FDA guidance on population pharmacokinetics similarly emphasizes that it helps identify differences in drug safety and supports dose selection, indicating that the field already has strong foundations for representing individual variability through population-level modeling [N3-R2]. The same guidance also highlights that this approach is used in drug development to support decisions about dose and regimen, which suggests that current methods are population-centric but still aim to encode individual differences [N3-R2].

In contrast, the evidence also shows that individual heterogeneity remains difficult to capture fully. Multi-omics integration is presented as a way to address limitations in panel-sequencing-based cancer drug response prediction, because genomic aberrations alone do not reflect the full complexity of tumor responses to drugs and because cancer is highly heterogeneous across patients and even within subtypes [N2-F2]. The study explicitly states that transcriptome information added on top of genomic panel features improves drug response prediction, which implies that current heterogeneity-aware methods rely on adding more molecular layers but still struggle with the full breadth of biological variation [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Another review notes that multi-omics integration is a major challenge in the field, with pivotal milestones including targeted sampling methods and artificial intelligence, and that this indicates ongoing difficulty in integrating heterogeneous data sources into coherent models [N2-R3]. A separate study on multi-omics modality completion and knowledge distillation for drug response prediction also notes that there are limitations in modeling heterogeneous responses and fusing complex multi-omics features [N2-R5].

This means the current approaches encode individual differences mainly through population-level summaries or through additional molecular layers such as transcriptome data, rather than through fully personalized, patient-specific models [N3-R1][N3-R5][N2-F2]. The tradeoff is therefore between generalizability across populations and the ability to make precise individual predictions: population methods are good for identifying common patterns and supporting dose optimization, but they do not by themselves capture the full individual heterogeneity that exists in real patients [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The cited evidence also suggests that current heterogeneity-aware methods are still limited by the need to integrate multiple omics modalities and by the difficulty of fusing them into a single predictive model [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Overall, the field is moving toward more comprehensive representation of individual differences, but the evidence indicates that these methods remain constrained by the availability of data, the complexity of multi-omics integration, and the fact that heterogeneity is not yet fully captured by any single approach [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The most plausible conclusion is that large models can contribute to heterogeneity-aware drug-effect studies by encoding individual differences through population-based or multi-omics-enhanced representations, but they are not yet sufficient to replace mechanistic, patient-specific modeling for personalized prediction [N3-R1][N3-R5][N2-F2].

Large models can already address several downstream tasks in drug effect simulation, but the evidence shows that their current capabilities are still constrained by biological scale, modality scope, and the strength of predictive/interpretive value.

The strongest evidence for downstream tasks comes from perturbation prediction and toxicity prediction. A recent primary research article describes XPert, a biologically informed dual-branch transformer model designed to model gene-specific perturbation effects and dose–response relationships, and states that it is used to predict drug-induced transcriptional perturbations by jointly modeling cellular contexts, multiscale drug properties, and dose–time dynamics [N1-F1]. This indicates that large models are being used for drug-induced perturbation effects, including dose-dependent responses and multi-dose-multi-time predictions [N1-F1]. The paper also notes that XPert supports generalization to unseen drugs and cells, and can be extended from large-scale preclinical data to clinical predictions, showing that these models are being deployed for both preclinical and translational use cases [N1-F1].

A complementary body of evidence shows that large models are being used for toxicity prediction. A primary research article in *Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling* explicitly states that large language models are being used as tools for molecular toxicity prediction, and that the study compared GPT-4 and GPT-4o with traditional deep-learning and machine-learning models, focusing on bone, neuro, and reproductive toxicity [N4-F3]. The abstract emphasizes that toxicity prediction is crucial in drug development and risk assessment, and that the study used GPT-4 combined with molecular docking techniques to study cardiotoxicity [N4-F3]. This indicates that large models are already being applied to toxicity prediction, including cardiotoxicity, and are being paired with other computational methods such as molecular docking to improve predictive power [N4-F3].

The evidence also points to broader downstream tasks beyond just toxicity or perturbation. A review on large language models for drug discovery and development states that LLMs can transform the field and that they are being explored for drug discovery and development more generally [N1-R2]. Another source notes that large models have demonstrated significant potential in assisting with the evaluation of pharmacokinetic properties, drug toxicity, and drug-drug interactions [N5-R3]. This supports the idea that large models are not confined to a single task but are being used across several related drug-effect tasks, including pharmacokinetic properties, toxicity, and drug-drug interactions [N1-R2][N5-R3].

On biological scales and modalities, the evidence shows that current large-model approaches can handle transcriptomic and multi-omics data as well as chemical and biological properties. XPert explicitly models chemical properties, biological properties, perturbation time, and dosage, and integrates prior knowledge such as drug–target interactions, protein–protein interactions, and drug–drug structure similarity into a knowledge-informed heterogeneous graph [N1-F1]. It also represents each cell as a “sentence” of gene tokens, with a global-cell-state token and gene tokens initialized with functional representation and binned expression values [N1-F1]. This suggests that the models can operate at the gene-level and cell-level, and can incorporate both biological and chemical modalities [N1-F1]. The same source also emphasizes that the model is designed to handle dose–time dynamics, showing that it can go beyond static predictions to capture dynamic drug effects [N1-F1].

In terms of predictive or interpretive value, the evidence is mixed. XPert is described as a transformer-based solution that excels in diverse scenarios including generalization to unseen drugs and cells and mdmt predictions, and that it supports a pretrain–fine-tune framework for extending preclinical data to clinical predictions [N1-F1]. This indicates strong predictive value for generalization and transferability [N1-F1]. However, the evidence also highlights limitations that constrain interpretive value. The paper notes that state-of-the-art approaches often concatenate chemical and cellular features and fail to resolve gene-specific responses, which suggests that some models may lack the interpretability needed to distinguish which genes are truly affected by a drug [N1-F1]. Another review notes that explainable AI methods are being developed for drug discovery, and that such methods are organized by input modality and degree of interpretability [N6-R2], which implies that interpretability remains an active area of research rather than a solved problem.

Overall, the current capabilities of large models for drug effect simulation are clear: they are being used for perturbation prediction, toxicity prediction, drug-drug interactions, and pharmacokinetic-related tasks, and they can handle transcriptomic, chemical, and biological modalities [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-R3]. However, the evidence also shows that their predictive value is strongest for generalization and transfer learning, while interpretive value remains limited and still requires explainable AI methods [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In short, large models can already contribute meaningfully to drug-effect simulation, but they are not yet fully biologically interpretable or universally predictive across all drug-effect contexts [N1-F1][N4-F3][N6-R2].

The field needs more integrated data types, better evaluation metrics, and stronger alignment with clinical and mechanistic validation to move toward a systematic, macro-level drug assessment system.

The evidence shows that missing data types and integration strategies are central to the current gap. Multi-omics integration is presented as a way to overcome limitations in panel-sequencing-based drug response prediction, because genomic aberrations alone do not reflect the full complexity of tumor responses to drugs and because cancer is highly heterogeneous [N2-F2]. The study explicitly states that transcriptome information added on top of genomic panel features improves drug response prediction, which indicates that the field still depends on adding more molecular layers rather than fully integrating all relevant data types [N2-R1][N2-F2]. A review on multi-omics integration further emphasizes that this is a major challenge in the field, with pivotal milestones including targeted sampling methods and artificial intelligence [N2-R3]. Another study on multi-omics modality completion and knowledge distillation for drug response prediction notes that there are limitations in modeling heterogeneous responses and fusing complex multi-omics features [N2-R5]. This suggests that the field still needs better strategies for combining heterogeneous data and handling missing or incomplete modalities [N2-R3][N2-R5].

The evidence also indicates that the current evaluation metrics are insufficient for a macro-level drug assessment system. The review on overcoming limitations in standard measures of drug response notes that there is a fundamental limitation in standard measures of drug sensitivity that hinders personalized prediction [N2-R2]. This implies that existing metrics are not robust enough to capture the full spectrum of drug effects needed for systematic assessment [N2-R2]. A related review on multi-omics integration notes that the field is evaluating challenges and milestones, including the use of artificial intelligence, but the cited evidence does not provide explicit metrics for biological plausibility or robustness beyond general statements about performance and integration [N2-R3]. For toxicity prediction, the cited study on large language models compares GPT-4 with traditional deep-learning and machine-learning models and reports performance comparisons, but it does not frame these as sufficient metrics for a macro-level assessment system [N4-F3]. The same study does emphasize that toxicity prediction is crucial in drug development and risk assessment [N4-F3], which suggests that the field needs more rigorous metrics than simple performance comparisons [N4-F3].

Alignment with clinical and mechanistic validation is another major gap. Population pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analysis is explicitly described as a tool for individualizing drug choice and dosing regimen, and as a method that supports dose selection, efficacy, and safety assessments [N3-R1][N3-R5]. FDA guidance on population pharmacokinetics similarly states that it helps identify differences in drug safety and supports dose selection [N3-R2]. These sources indicate that mechanistic validation is already part of the field, but the evidence also shows that current methods are still population-centric and do not fully translate into real-world outcomes [N3-R1][N3-R2]. A review on pharmacometrics and drug development states that LLMs have demonstrated significant potential in assisting with pharmacokinetic properties, drug toxicity, and drug-drug interactions, but it does not explicitly state that these capabilities are yet validated in clinical settings [N5-R3]. The same source also notes that LLMs are being explored as tools in pharmacometrics, suggesting that mechanistic and translational validation remain important but are not yet fully established [N5-R1][N5-R3].

A related point is that clinical validation should bridge simulation and real-world outcomes. The evidence on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling and simulation states that four elements are crucial to successful PK/PD modeling and simulation for efficient and effective rational drug development [N7-R1]. This implies that validation should include not only internal consistency but also external validation against real-world data [N7-R1]. A review on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic-driven drug development further notes deficiencies in how PK/PD studies are conducted and suggests new strategies to bridge the gap between preclinical and clinical development [N7-R2]. This supports the conclusion that clinical validation must explicitly connect simulated drug effects to clinical outcomes, biomarkers, and endpoints [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug, while pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body, which reinforces the need for validation that spans both PK and PD dimensions [N7-R4].

In summary, the field needs more comprehensive data integration across modalities, better metrics for biological plausibility and robustness, and stronger clinical and mechanistic validation to support a macro-level drug assessment system [N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The current evidence suggests that multi-omics, toxicity prediction, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic methods are promising, but they are still limited by missing data types, insufficient evaluation metrics, and weak alignment with real-world clinical outcomes [N2-F2][N4-F3][N7-R1].

Large models currently produce some interpretable mechanistic insights, but their biological plausibility is still limited and the main gaps lie in biological consistency, missing causal structure, and the ability to explain complex drug effects.

The evidence shows that large models can generate interpretable mechanistic insights. XPert is described as a biologically informed model that jointly models cellular contexts, multiscale drug properties, and dose–time dynamics, and that it uses a dual-branch architecture to capture both intrinsic gene–gene interactions and extrinsic chemical perturbation effects [N1-F1]. The paper also states that the model is augmented by a knowledge-informed heterogeneous graph that bridges chemical–biological spaces and by condition tokens that encode nonlinear dose–time responses [N1-F1]. This suggests that the model is designed not just to predict outcomes but also to encode mechanistic relationships, which can support interpretation of which genes and pathways are affected by a drug [N1-F1].

A separate line of evidence supports explainability in drug discovery. A review on explainable AI methods for drug discovery introduces a multidimensional taxonomy of XAI approaches tailored to drug discovery, and it explicitly states that methods are organized by input modality, degree of interpretability, and other factors [N6-R2]. This indicates that the field is actively trying to make AI models in drug discovery more interpretable, and that interpretability is being treated as a structured research problem rather than an afterthought [N6-R2]. Another study on identifying plausible adverse drug reactions using knowledge-based methods states that many predicted paths are consistent across all drugs and could support a plausible biological mechanism for a predicted effect [N6-R3]. This suggests that some models can produce interpretable, biologically meaningful pathways or mechanisms that align with known biology [N6-R3].

Despite these advances, the evidence also highlights major gaps in biological plausibility. XPert’s paper notes that state-of-the-art approaches often concatenate chemical and cellular features and fail to resolve gene-specific responses, which implies that some models may obscure the biological mechanisms they are supposed to capture [N1-F1]. The same paper also emphasizes that dose–time dynamics are inadequately modeled in previous work, with simplistic encodings such as one-hot encoding being insufficient for nonlinear dose–response relationships [N1-F1]. This indicates that current large models can produce interpretable outputs, but those outputs may still lack the biological detail needed to explain complex drug effects accurately [N1-F1].

The evidence further suggests that biological plausibility is constrained by missing causal structure and by the need to connect computational predictions to real biological knowledge. The review on multi-omics integration notes that the field is navigating challenges while spotlighting pivotal milestones such as targeted sampling methods and artificial intelligence [N2-R3]. This implies that even when models are more interpretable, they may still rely on incomplete biological knowledge and may not fully capture the causal relationships underlying drug responses [N2-R3]. The study on multi-omics-driven kinetic modeling states that kinetic models offer a systems-level solution to address limitations by simulating drug administration and tracking how interventions affect metabolism, but the excerpt provided here does not explicitly resolve whether large models can yet achieve the same level of causal plausibility as kinetic models [N2-R4]. However, the fact that kinetic modeling is being used as a systems-level solution suggests that current large models are still not sufficient to replace mechanistic models in all cases [N2-R4].

Overall, the current evidence indicates that large models can produce some interpretable mechanistic insights, particularly when they are explicitly designed with biological knowledge and structured to model gene interactions, dose–time dynamics, and heterogeneous graphs [N1-F1][N6-R2]. However, their biological plausibility remains limited by the fact that they often fail to resolve gene-specific responses, rely on simplistic feature encodings, and may not fully capture causal relationships or nonlinear biological effects [N1-F1]. The main gaps are therefore in biological consistency, causal structure, and the ability to explain complex drug effects that depend on nonlinear dose–time relationships and multi-omics interactions [N1-F1][N2-R3].
node_outputs.N12:
Large models have potential for clinical feasibility, but validation must bridge simulation with real-world outcomes, and regulatory and translational barriers remain substantial.

The clinical endpoints and biomarkers most relevant to large-model validation are those that connect simulation to drug effect and safety. Pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) analysis is explicitly described as a tool for individualizing drug choice and dosing regimen, and it supports dose selection, efficacy, and safety assessments [N3-R1][N3-R5]. FDA guidance on population pharmacokinetics similarly states that it helps identify differences in drug safety and supports dose selection [N3-R2]. These sources indicate that the most relevant endpoints for clinical validation are safety-related differences, dose selection, and the relationship between exposure and response [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The same guidance also emphasizes that population pharmacokinetics is used in drug development to support decisions about dose and regimen, which reinforces that clinical biomarkers should include pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic markers rather than only static molecular features [N3-R2].

Validation should bridge simulation with real-world outcomes through both internal and external validation. The evidence on PK/PD modeling and simulation states that four elements are crucial to successful PK/PD modeling and simulation for efficient and effective rational drug development [N7-R1]. This implies that validation must include not only model fit to training data but also robustness across different populations, doses, and disease states [N7-R1]. A review on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic-driven drug development notes deficiencies in how PK/PD studies are conducted and suggests new strategies to bridge the gap between preclinical and clinical development [N7-R2]. This supports the idea that validation should explicitly compare simulated outcomes with clinical endpoints, biomarker measurements, and real-world patient data [N7-R1][N7-R2].

The evidence also indicates that large models need to be validated using a broader set of outcomes than just toxicity prediction. The study on large language models as tools for molecular toxicity prediction emphasizes that toxicity prediction is crucial in drug development and risk assessment, and that GPT-4 was compared with traditional models for bone, neuro, and reproductive toxicity [N4-F3]. This suggests that toxicity-related biomarkers are important, but the same study also highlights that the field needs performance comparisons across modalities and that the approach holds promise for reducing development costs and improving patient safety [N4-F3]. In other words, clinical validation should not be limited to one endpoint but should include a range of biomarkers relevant to efficacy, safety, and toxicity [N4-F3].

Regulatory and translational barriers are considerable. The EMA guidelines on clinical pharmacology and pharmacokinetics help medicine developers prepare marketing authorisation, which implies that regulatory acceptance is tied to standardized evidence and endpoints that are recognized by authorities [N7-R5]. A review on AI in drug development notes that AI is increasingly deployed to address key drug development challenges, including multiomic data integration, structural biology, pharmacokinetic prediction, and toxicity [N7-R3]. This indicates that regulatory barriers include the need to demonstrate reproducibility, explainability, and consistency with established pharmacological principles [N7-R3]. The same source also suggests that AI is poised to revolutionize drug development, but that this requires overcoming the usual regulatory and translational hurdles of validation and approval [N7-R3].

In addition, the evidence suggests that clinical feasibility depends on translational barriers such as data quality and clinical applicability. ## Integrated assessment: can large models now simulate drug effects, and how the field is likely to evolve?

The short answer is: **yes, but only partially and with important limitations**. Large models already contribute to drug-effect simulation by addressing several downstream tasks, including perturbation prediction, toxicity prediction, and related pharmacokinetic/toxicity tasks. They can operate across molecular, transcriptomic, and chemical modalities, and some models are designed to encode dose–time dynamics and gene-level interactions. However, the evidence also shows that their current capabilities are still constrained by biological scale, interpretive depth, and the ability to fully capture individual heterogeneity. The field is therefore likely to evolve toward more integrated, clinically validated, and mechanistically grounded systems, rather than toward a single “silver bullet” model that replaces traditional pharmacological approaches.

---

## 1. What large models can currently do for drug effect simulation

The evidence indicates that large models are already being used for several downstream tasks relevant to drug effect simulation:

- **Perturbation prediction**: XPert is described as a biologically informed dual-branch transformer model designed to model gene-specific perturbation effects and dose–response relationships. It predicts drug-induced transcriptional perturbations by jointly modeling cellular contexts, multiscale drug properties, and dose–time dynamics [N1-F1]. This means large models are already being used to simulate how drugs alter gene expression and how those changes depend on dose and timing [N1-F1].
- **Toxicity prediction**: Large language models are being used as tools for molecular toxicity prediction, with one study comparing GPT-4 and GPT-4o with traditional models and focusing on bone, neuro, and reproductive toxicity [N4-F3]. Another part of the evidence notes that these models are also used in combination with molecular docking techniques to study cardiotoxicity [N4-F3].
- **Broader drug-effect tasks**: A review states that large language models can transform drug discovery and development, and another source notes that LLMs have demonstrated significant potential in assisting with pharmacokinetic properties, drug toxicity, and drug-drug interactions [N1-R2][N5-R3]. This suggests that large models are not confined to one specific task, but are being used across multiple drug-effect domains.

In terms of biological scales and modalities, the evidence shows that current models can handle transcriptomic, chemical, and biological modalities. XPert explicitly models chemical properties, biological properties, perturbation time, and dosage, and integrates prior knowledge such as drug–target interactions, protein–protein interactions, and drug–drug structure similarity into a knowledge-informed heterogeneous graph [N1-F1]. It also represents each cell as a “sentence” of gene tokens, with a global-cell-state token and gene tokens initialized with functional representation and binned expression values [N1-F1]. This indicates that the models can operate at the gene-level and cell-level, and can incorporate both biological and chemical data [N1-F1].

As for predictive and interpretive value, the evidence is mixed. XPert is described as a transformer-based solution that excels in generalization to unseen drugs and cells and in multi-dose-multi-time predictions, and that it supports a pretrain–fine-tune framework for extending preclinical data to clinical predictions [N1-F1]. This suggests strong predictive value for generalization and transfer learning. However, the same evidence also highlights limitations that constrain interpretive value: state-of-the-art approaches often concatenate chemical and cellular features and fail to resolve gene-specific responses, implying that some models may not clearly distinguish which genes are truly affected by a drug [N1-F1]. A separate review on explainable AI methods for drug discovery states that methods are organized by input modality and degree of interpretability, indicating that interpretability remains an active but still developing area of research [N6-R2].

So, the current capabilities are **meaningful but not yet comprehensive**: large models can simulate drug effects, predict toxicity, and contribute to pharmacokinetic and drug-drug interaction tasks, but they are still limited in how well they explain complex biological mechanisms and how robustly they generalize across all drug-effect contexts [N1-F1][N4-F3][N6-R2].

---

## 2. How well heterogeneity is captured by current approaches

Current approaches do encode individual differences, but they do so in ways that still reflect important tradeoffs between **population-level generalization** and **personalized prediction**.

The evidence shows that **population pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PKPD) analysis is explicitly designed to individualize drug choice and dosing regimen** [N3-R1]. It also supports dose selection, efficacy, and safety assessments, and FDA guidance on population pharmacokinetics emphasizes that it helps identify differences in drug safety [N3-R2][N3-R5]. This means that the field already has strong foundations for representing individual variability through population-based modeling.

However, the evidence also shows that individual heterogeneity remains difficult to capture fully. **Multi-omics integration is presented as a way to overcome limitations in panel-sequencing-based cancer drug response prediction**, because genomic aberrations alone do not reflect the full complexity of tumor responses to drugs and because cancer is highly heterogeneous [N2-F2]. The study explicitly states that transcriptome information added on top of genomic panel features improves drug response prediction, which implies that current heterogeneity-aware methods rely on adding more molecular layers rather than fully integrating all relevant data [N2-R1][N2-F2]. A review notes that multi-omics integration is a major challenge in the field, with pivotal milestones including targeted sampling methods and artificial intelligence [N2-R3]. Another study on multi-omics modality completion and knowledge distillation for drug response prediction notes limitations in modeling heterogeneous responses and fusing complex multi-omics features [N2-R5].

This means the current approaches encode individual differences mainly through **population-level summaries or through additional molecular layers such as transcriptome data**, rather than through fully personalized, patient-specific models [N3-R1][N3-R5][N2-F2]. The tradeoff is therefore between generalizability across populations and the ability to make precise individual predictions: population methods are good for identifying common patterns and supporting dose optimization, but they do not by themselves capture the full individual heterogeneity that exists in real patients [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The cited evidence also suggests that current heterogeneity-aware methods are still limited by the need to integrate multiple omics modalities and by the difficulty of fusing them into a single predictive model [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Overall, the evidence indicates that large models can contribute to heterogeneity-aware drug-effect studies by encoding individual differences through population-based or multi-omics-enhanced representations, but they are not yet sufficient to replace mechanistic, patient-specific modeling for personalized prediction [N3-R1][N3-R5][N2-F2].

---

## 3. What the field needs to move toward a systematic, macro-level drug assessment system

The evidence suggests that the field needs **more integrated data types, better evaluation metrics, and stronger alignment with clinical and mechanistic validation** to move toward a systematic, macro-level drug assessment system.

### Missing data types and integration strategies
The evidence shows that multi-omics integration is still needed to address limitations in panel-sequencing-based drug response prediction, because genomic aberrations alone do not reflect the full complexity of tumor responses to drugs and because cancer is highly heterogeneous [N2-F2]. The study also shows that transcriptome information added on top of genomic panel features improves drug response prediction, indicating that current methods still depend on adding more molecular layers rather than fully integrating all relevant data types [N2-R1][N2-F2]. A review notes that multi-omics integration is a major challenge in the field, with pivotal milestones including targeted sampling methods and artificial intelligence [N2-R3]. Another study notes limitations in modeling heterogeneous responses and fusing complex multi-omics features [N2-R5]. So, the field still needs better strategies for combining heterogeneous data and handling missing or incomplete modalities [N2-R3][N2-R5].

### Evaluation metrics needed for biological plausibility and robustness
The evidence also indicates that current evaluation metrics are insufficient for a macro-level drug assessment system. A review on overcoming limitations in standard measures of drug response notes that there is a fundamental limitation in standard measures of drug sensitivity that hinders personalized prediction [N2-R2]. This implies that existing metrics are not robust enough to capture the full spectrum of drug effects needed for systematic assessment [N2-R2]. While the cited study on toxicity prediction compares GPT-4 with traditional models and reports performance comparisons [N4-F3], the evidence does not frame these as sufficient metrics for a macro-level system, suggesting that more rigorous metrics than simple performance comparisons are needed [N4-F3].

### Alignment with clinical and mechanistic validation
A major gap is alignment with clinical and mechanistic validation. Population PK/PD analysis is explicitly described as a tool for individualizing drug choice and dosing regimen, and as a method that supports dose selection, efficacy, and safety assessments [N3-R1][N3-R5]. FDA guidance on population pharmacokinetics similarly states that it helps identify differences in drug safety and supports dose selection [N3-R2]. These sources indicate that mechanistic validation is already part of the field, but the evidence also shows that current methods are still population-centric and do not fully translate into real-world outcomes [N3-R1][N3-R2]. A review on pharmacometrics and drug development states that LLMs have demonstrated significant potential in assisting with pharmacokinetic properties, drug toxicity, and drug-drug interactions, but it does not explicitly state that these capabilities are yet validated in clinical settings [N5-R3]. This suggests that mechanistic and translational validation remain important but are not yet fully established [N5-R1][N5-R3].

The evidence also emphasizes that clinical validation should bridge simulation with real-world outcomes. The evidence on PK/PD modeling and simulation states that four elements are crucial to successful PK/PD modeling and simulation for efficient and effective rational drug development [N7-R1]. This implies that validation must include not only internal consistency but also external validation against real-world data [N7-R1]. A review on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic-driven drug development notes deficiencies in how PK/PD studies are conducted and suggests new strategies to bridge the gap between preclinical and clinical development [N7-R2]. This supports the conclusion that validation should explicitly connect simulated drug effects to clinical outcomes, biomarkers, and endpoints [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug, while pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body, which reinforces the need for validation that spans both PK and PD dimensions [N7-R4].

In short, the field needs more comprehensive integration across modalities, better metrics for biological plausibility and robustness, and stronger clinical and mechanistic validation to support a macro-level drug assessment system [N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2].

---

## 4. How interpretable and biologically plausible large models are in practice

The evidence shows that large models can produce some **interpretable mechanistic insights**, but their **biological plausibility is still limited**, with the main gaps lying in **biological consistency, missing causal structure, and the ability to explain complex drug effects**.

XPert is described as a biologically informed model that jointly models cellular contexts, multiscale drug properties, and dose–time dynamics, and that it uses a dual-branch architecture to capture both intrinsic gene–gene interactions and extrinsic chemical perturbation effects [N1-F1]. It is also augmented by a knowledge-informed heterogeneous graph that bridges chemical–biological spaces and by condition tokens that encode nonlinear dose–time responses [N1-F1]. This suggests that the model is designed not only to predict outcomes but also to encode mechanistic relationships, which can support interpretation of which genes and pathways are affected by a drug [N1-F1].

A separate line of evidence supports explainability in drug discovery. A review on explainable AI methods for drug discovery introduces a multidimensional taxonomy of XAI approaches tailored to drug discovery, and it explicitly states that methods are organized by input modality, degree of interpretability, and other factors [N6-R2]. This indicates that the field is actively trying to make AI models in drug discovery more interpretable, and that interpretability is being treated as a structured research problem rather than an afterthought [N6-R2]. Another study on identifying plausible adverse drug reactions using knowledge-based methods states that many predicted paths are consistent across all drugs and could support a plausible biological mechanism for a predicted effect [N6-R3]. This suggests that some models can produce interpretable, biologically meaningful pathways or mechanisms that align with known biology [N6-R3].

Despite these advances, the evidence also highlights major gaps in biological plausibility. XPert’s paper notes that state-of-the-art approaches often concatenate chemical and cellular features and fail to resolve gene-specific responses, which implies that some models may obscure the biological mechanisms they are supposed to capture [N1-F1]. The same paper also emphasizes that dose–time dynamics are inadequately modeled in previous work, with simplistic encodings such as one-hot encoding being insufficient for nonlinear dose–response relationships [N1-F1]. This indicates that current large models can produce interpretable outputs, but those outputs may still lack the biological detail needed to explain complex drug effects accurately [N1-F1].

The evidence further suggests that biological plausibility is constrained by missing causal structure and by the need to connect computational predictions to real biological knowledge. The review on multi-omics integration notes that the field is navigating challenges while spotlighting pivotal milestones such as targeted sampling methods and artificial intelligence [N2-R3]. This implies that even when models are more interpretable, they may still rely on incomplete biological knowledge and may not fully capture the causal relationships underlying drug responses [N2-R3]. The study on multi-omics-driven kinetic modeling states that kinetic models offer a systems-level solution to address limitations by simulating drug administration and tracking how interventions affect metabolism, but the excerpt provided here does not explicitly resolve whether large models can yet achieve the same level of causal plausibility as kinetic models [N2-R4]. However, the fact that kinetic modeling is being used as a systems-level solution suggests that current large models are still not sufficient to replace mechanistic models in all cases [N2-R4].

Overall, the current evidence indicates that large models can produce some interpretable mechanistic insights, particularly when they are explicitly designed with biological knowledge and structured to model gene interactions, dose–time dynamics, and heterogeneous graphs [N1-F1][N6-R2]. However, their biological plausibility remains limited by the fact that they often fail to resolve gene-specific responses, rely on simplistic feature encodings, and may not fully capture causal relationships or nonlinear biological effects [N1-F1]. The main gaps are therefore in biological consistency, causal structure, and the ability to explain complex drug effects that depend on nonlinear dose–time relationships and multi-omics interactions [N1-F1][N2-R3].

---

## 5. What makes large models clinically feasible and how validation should be done

Large models have potential for clinical feasibility, but validation must bridge simulation with real-world outcomes, and regulatory and translational barriers remain substantial.

The most relevant clinical endpoints and biomarkers are those that connect simulation to drug effect and safety. Pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) analysis is explicitly described as a tool for individualizing drug choice and dosing regimen, and it supports dose selection, efficacy, and safety assessments [N3-R1][N3-R5]. FDA guidance on population pharmacokinetics similarly states that it helps identify differences in drug safety and supports dose selection [N3-R2]. These sources indicate that the most relevant endpoints for clinical validation are safety-related differences, dose selection, and the relationship between exposure and response [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The same guidance also emphasizes that population pharmacokinetics is used in drug development to support decisions about dose and regimen, which reinforces that clinical biomarkers should include pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic markers rather than only static molecular features [N3-R2].

Validation should bridge simulation with real-world outcomes through both internal and external validation. The evidence on PK/PD modeling and simulation states that four elements are crucial to successful PK/PD modeling and simulation for efficient and effective rational drug development [N7-R1]. This implies that validation must include not only model fit to training data but also robustness across different populations, doses, and disease states [N7-R1]. A review on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic-driven drug development notes deficiencies in how PK/PD studies are conducted and suggests new strategies to bridge the gap between preclinical and clinical development [N7-R2]. This supports the idea that validation should explicitly compare simulated outcomes with clinical endpoints, biomarker measurements, and real-world patient data [N7-R1][N7-R2].

The evidence also indicates that large models need to be validated using a broader set of outcomes than just toxicity prediction. The study on large language models as tools for molecular toxicity prediction emphasizes that toxicity prediction is crucial in drug development and risk assessment, and that GPT-4 was compared with traditional models for bone, neuro, and reproductive toxicity [N4-F3]. This suggests that toxicity-related biomarkers are important, but the same study also highlights that the field needs performance comparisons across modalities and that the approach holds promise for reducing development costs and improving patient safety [N4-F3]. In other words, clinical validation should not be limited to one endpoint but should include a range of biomarkers relevant to efficacy, safety, and toxicity [N4-F3].

Regulatory and translational barriers are considerable. The EMA guidelines on clinical pharmacology and pharmacokinetics help medicine developers prepare marketing authorisation, which implies that regulatory acceptance is tied to standardized evidence and endpoints that are recognized by authorities [N7-R5]. A review on AI in drug development notes that AI is increasingly deployed to address key drug development challenges, including multiomic data integration, structural biology, pharmacokinetic prediction, and toxicity [N7-R3]. This indicates that regulatory barriers include the need to demonstrate reproducibility, explainability, and consistency with established pharmacological principles [N7-R3]. The same source also suggests that AI is poised to revolutionize drug development, but that this requires overcoming the usual regulatory and translational hurdles of validation and approval [N7-R3].

In addition, the evidence suggests that clinical feasibility depends on translational barriers such as data quality and clinical applicability. The review on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic-driven drug development emphasizes deficiencies in current PK/PD studies and the need for new strategies to bridge preclinical and clinical development [N7-R2]. This implies that large models must not only simulate drug effects in vitro or in preclinical models but must also be validated in clinical settings where patient variability, confounding factors, and real-world pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic behavior are present [N7-R2]. The evidence on toxicity prediction also shows that while GPT-4 is comparable to traditional models in certain areas, the study is still focused on molecular toxicity and does not provide evidence that large models can yet support full clinical decision-making [N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence suggests that large models have potential for clinical feasibility if they are validated against PK/PD endpoints, safety biomarkers, and real-world outcomes [N3-R1][N3-R5][N7-R1]. However, validation must be rigorous and bridge simulation with clinical data, and regulatory and translational barriers remain substantial because the field still needs standardized endpoints, reproducibility, and approval-compatible evidence [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

---

## 6. How the field is likely to evolve

Putting all the evidence together, the most plausible evolution path is **not** toward a single perfect large model that replaces all traditional pharmacological methods, but toward a **more integrated, interpretable, and clinically validated system**.

### Likely direction 1: More integrated models
The field is likely to move toward models that combine **multi-omics, mechanistic knowledge, and large-model inference**. XPert already demonstrates that biologically informed architecture and heterogeneous graph modeling can improve perturbation prediction [N1-F1]. The evidence on multi-omics integration also indicates that targeted sampling methods and artificial intelligence are pivotal milestones [N2-R3]. This suggests that future systems will be more integrated across data types and more explicitly linked to biological knowledge [N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Likely direction 2: Better evaluation and validation
The field will need better evaluation metrics for biological plausibility, robustness, and clinical relevance. The evidence shows that current metrics are insufficient and that validation must bridge simulation with real-world outcomes [N2-R2][N4-F3][N7-R1]. The likely result is more rigorous benchmarking, cross-validation across populations and endpoints, and closer alignment with clinical and pharmacodynamic endpoints [N7-R1][N7-R2].

### Likely direction 3: More explainable and interpretable models
Explainable AI methods are already being developed for drug discovery, and mechanistic insights are increasingly being sought [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence indicates that interpretability is still an active research area, and that current models can produce interpretable mechanistic insights while still lacking full causal plausibility [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The future is therefore likely to include more interpretable models and better documentation of which biological relationships they capture and which remain uncertain [N1-F1][N6-R2].

### Likely direction 4: Stronger clinical and regulatory alignment
Clinical feasibility will depend on stronger alignment with regulatory expectations and real-world validation. The evidence suggests that EMA guidelines and PK/PD validation frameworks are important for clinical translation [N7-R5]. The field is likely to evolve toward models that can be validated against standardized endpoints, demonstrate reproducibility, and meet regulatory expectations for safety, efficacy, and toxicology [N7-R3][N7-R5].

---

## Conclusion

**Yes, large models can already simulate drug effects in several meaningful ways**, especially for perturbation prediction, toxicity prediction, and related pharmacokinetic/toxicity tasks. They can handle transcriptomic, chemical, and biological data, and some models are designed to encode dose–time dynamics and gene-level interactions [N1-F1][N4-F3]. But **they are not yet sufficient on their own** to fully replace traditional pharmacological methods. Their current limitations include incomplete biological plausibility, limited interpretability, and the need for better integration across omics modalities and clinical endpoints [N1-F1][N2-R3][N6-R2].

The field is therefore likely to evolve toward **more integrated, interpretable, and clinically validated systems** that combine large models with mechanistic knowledge, multi-omics data, and rigorous validation against real-world outcomes. In this future, large models will remain important tools, but they will be part of a broader pipeline rather than a standalone solution [N1-F1][N2-R3][N7-R1].
